newsitem.title: COMOROS: Comoros releases passengers held in hijack case.
newsitem.headline: Comoros releases passengers held in hijack case.

text.p: The authorities in the Comoro islands on Saturday released two passengers held for a week for questioning about the hijacking of an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767.

The passengers, Kenyan businessman Micheal Odenyo and Djiboutian trade unionist Souleimane Ahmed Mohamed, survived when the plane crashed into the sea on November 23 but other passengers then erroneously identified them as hijackers.
"I do not know really what has been more painful -- the crash or the incarceration," Mohamed told Reuters on Saturday. "But we have not been physically tortured," he added.
"They are exonerated and no charge is held against them," public prosecutor Cheikh Salim told Reuters.
The passengers will leave the Comoros later on Saturday on an Emirates flight to Dubai.
At the site of the crash, just off a beach on the main island of Grande Comore, rescue workers and local officials held a memorial service for the dead on Saturday.
Boats which took part in the rescue last weekend slowly circled the spot where the tail and one engine of the plane poke out of the crystal-clear water.
"This is our way of paying respect to those who died," said Caroline Fotherby, assistant manager of a local diving club.
Mourners scattered palm wreaths and flowers on the sea while a Roman Catholic priest prayed and sprinkled holy water.
Sultan Mohammed, one of six Ethiopian airline officials at the ceremony, also threw a bouquet onto the water.
"It's been very tragic and sad. We appreciate these people's assistance and this tribute," he told Reuters.
The beach is still sealed off from the public and guarded by soldiers and police.

Back in Moroni Cheikh Salim said the co-pilot of the plane, Yonas Mekuria, had identied the bodies of two of the three hijackers among the 125 people killed in the crash. Fifty people survived the accident.
There was no immediate word on when the Comoran authorities would release the bodies to their relatives. They have said they plan to keep them until all have been identified.

Officials sources said on Saturday that the Comoros, a small archipelago state in the Indian Ocean, had turned down U.S. and British requests for access to the flight recorders. The government is waiting for advice on the subject from international civil aviation authorities.
